Finally, the market is coming to our previously uncommon view that the ECB still has room to cut this year. Reaction functions still matter, but the data matter more. And increasingly, the data are telling very different stories. In the US, inflation is back in the driver’s seat for the Fed. With macro data solid and possibly picking up, markets have begun to contemplate two way risks for policy, particularly if aggregate demand reaccelerates inflation. We see little scope for a hike this year for a few key reasons. First, productivity growth has been stronger than expected, meaning the underlying demand has yet to create new inflationary pressures. Second, and consequently, underlying inflation still seems to be trending lower, and we expect tariff-driven inflation to peak soon and then fade. And while downside risks appear diminished for now in the labor market, the same productivity gains should limit much larger pickup in labor demand. Further, consumption spending is already elevated relative to wealth-implied levels, so that key engine of demand may not have much further to run. So, investors should put some probability on no cuts from the Fed this year, and the Minutes note limited tolerance for upside inflationary surprises, but our baseline view of two more cuts remains. But the tension of current versus expected inflation explains the consistently close MPC votes. Markets shifted only recently toward a clear easing bias when the labor market data surprised to the downside. Weak productivity has been notable, so labor market softening is needed for inflationary pressures to ease. Private sector wage growth has already come down, and we expect services inflation to fall notably. Against that backdrop, easing is becoming more defensible, even if the path remains gradual. But an informative contrast exists between Australia and the Euro area. The RBA has reversed course. Raising rates followed inflation concerns, but partly because monetary policy had been loose as the fiscal impulse strengthened. Markets briefly entertained a similar rate hike narrative in the euro area, a view we consistently pushed back on. Recent ECB communication has shifted the market pricing closer to our base case for further cuts. The comparison with Australia is instructive. While fiscal support and weak productivity echo the Australian story, euro area wage growth is decelerating. Moreover, our estimate of the neutral rate is below the ECB’s estimate, and holding rates steady would likely push inflation below target over the forecast horizon. In the last three days following the middle east tension, Korean interest rates have experienced an aggressive selloff due to market concerns about inflationary dynamics, driven by high oil prices and a weak currency. We are now pricing in approximately 50bp of rate hikes over the next year and an additional 25bp of rate hikes in the second year. Historically, the shock from surging oil prices results in a flattening of the yield curve, as the front-end sells off amid inflation concerns, while the long- end outperforms due to the negative impact on growth. We have observed this same phenomenon this time with the 2s10s curve flattening over the last few days. Looking ahead, if oil prices continue to rise, we expect the curve to bear-steepen in the 1s5s segment, as it is challenging for the market to price in more than two hikes in one year. Additionally, discussions about fiscal support, such as fuel tax cuts and other economic measures to boost exports, could also push rates higher in the belly of the curve, as the market will need to price in potential fiscal slippage. records.text: Eastern Europe (CEE): higher oil and risk off to challenge rate cuts If higher energy prices are prolonged, the opportunity for regional central banks to cut rates will be delayed (Hungary, Romania) or diminished (Czechia, Poland). CEE countries are net importers of energy, and higher oil will be reflected in pump prices relatively quickly. Gas developments will also be key to be watched – though impact will be lagged – for inflation (Czechia and Poland) and/or the budget (Hungary and Romania). Every 10% increase in oil in local currency terms could increase headline inflation via fuel prices by 0.1-0.25pp, with Czechia at the low end, Hungary and Poland in the middle, and Romania at the higher end. The impact on Hungary’s monetary policy is exacerbated during this risk-off period given the heavy Hungarian Forint (HUF) long positioning and high caution by the central bank pre-elections. The 24 March rate decision may see an on-hold decision, but we still see decent room to cut rates after 12 April elections towards 5% by 2027. Elsewhere, we see upside risks to our YE2026 policy rate forecasts, currently at 3.0% in Czechia, 3.0% in Poland, and 5.25% in Romania. Balance of payments/fiscal risks could likely be limited as long as there is no major and prolonged spillover to gas. We estimate that every US$10/bbl increase in crude prices, all else equal, could raise CEE’s oil import bill by c.0.1-0.15% of GDP, with Hungary and Poland slightly more sensitive than peers. records.text: European Rates Weekly 05 March 2026 Citi Research 6 € curve: the convexity awakening We look at the historical impact of richer short-expiry vols on the shape of the € swap curve. We present two results: (i) the most effective hedge has been paying 10s against either 2s or 5s and 30s, but this doesn’t take into account the cost of rolling the position to spot and (ii) investors expecting a further increase in vol over the next week should receive 2s30s. All you need is a commodity shock (to revive gamma). This week’s moves in € swap rates have been dramatic, fuelled by the sharp re-pricing in oil and gas prices (on how these may map into higher EA consumer inflation, see our economists’ take here). Despite the move being front-end driven (with the 2y rate selling off week-to-date at the fastest pace in 17 months), sharp swings in the level of the term structure also mechanically impact long-end rates via changes in the value of convexity. While the static effect of the change in duration is second-order relative to the change in PV, self-reinforcing dynamics can lead to a meaningful change in the slope of the long-end curve. T o the extent that we can proxy the (unobserved) realized volatility via short-expiry implied volatility, we can directly quantify the impact of convexity demand on the shape of the € swap curve. Systematically receiving 5s10s30s has historically hedged 60% of short-expiry vol’s monthly swings. We therefore run structurally negative convexity strategies

Of the 31 provinces, 12 have explicitly pledged to achieve a carbon peak before 2030 in their 15th FYPs, while another two provinces, Jiangsu and Jilin, have stated that they will complete the carbon reduction tasks assigned by the central government during the 15th FYP period. These developments suggest that authorities will still pursue the 2030 carbon goal. We believe that the 2030 goal is unlikely to have a significant impact on the economy during the 15th FYP period, as it requires China's total carbon emissions to peak before 2030, without specifying the peak level. In other words, the authorities could set relatively modest carbon reduction targets in the initial years of the FYP, letting total carbon emissions climb further (resulting in a high base), and then intensify their reduction efforts towards the end of the FYP so as to reach the targeted peak. The real challenge of carbon peaking, in our view, lies in the 16th FYP period (2031–35), as after the 2030 peak is reached, China will have to keep cutting carbon emissions per unit of GDP faster than the national GDP growth each year during the 16th FYP. It is also a function of a relatively flat estimated Phillips curve, which implies that the pass through from changes in economic activity / unemployment to inflation is muted. The immunity of core inflation to energy price shocks is not assured, however. Fed research following the energy price shock in 2022 , which was triggered by the Russian invasion of Ukraine , indicated that there could be second -order effects that lead to a more persistent rise in core inflation. The authors (see here) conclude, “our analysis suggests that increases in oil prices lead to small but significant second-round effects on inflation through their pass -through to food and core prices, and that these effects operate with long lags.” The Fed’s response and long-term interest rates These simulations show that oil price shocks similar to those outlined above are initially a modest dovish impulse for the Fed. records.text: M Global Idea 2 Will Higher Oil Break Correlations (Again)? Equities and bonds selling off together on Monday sparked by the conflict in Iran have brought up the spectre of markets coming out of the pandemic, when stocks-UST returns correlation stayed stubbornly positive. Back then, 60/40 equity-bond portfolios saw the worst annual performance in nearly a century, and the scars of that experience run so deep that even now, several years on, we often have long debates with investors on whether bonds work as diversifiers. Those discussions almost always begin with the question, "Are correlations broken?" That question has now reared its ugly head again. Our answer is that even in an environment like this, equity-bond correlations can remain intact and bonds can diversify risk, but with important caveats: • it depends on how oil supply disruptions on the back of the conflict in Middle East could impact growth and inflation longer term, and • some bonds work better than others in cushioning portfolios when equities sell off – not all safe havens are built the same. Wait, what's oil got to do with correlations? As we've pointed out over the past few years, the 'classic' negative correlation between stock and bond returns is underpinned by the 'traditional' relationship of growth and inflation travelling in the same direction: stocks offset losses in bonds as growth rises alongside inflation, and vice versa. . We like long ILS against EUR. The shekel has historically strengthened during periods of regional tension because Israel’s external position generates inflows in stress rather than outflows. Israel runs current -account surplus and its residents hold large foreign assets, so uncertainty tends to trigger repatriation and FX hedging into ILS. At the same time, Israel’s USD-earning tech exports are largely insulated from regional conflict, and exporters typically convert dollar revenues into shekels to meet domestic costs when risk rises. Heading into the latest Middle East conflict, investor positioning in IL S was already extremely underweight (Figure 3), while the increase in perceived risk has so far been less severe than during the 12-Day War in mid-2025. If the war proves short -lived, the economic impact on Israel should be limited, and there is a reasonable chance that Israel ultimately emerges in a stronger strategic position, given the significant weakening of Iran’s military and proxy capabilities. A future nuclear deal, if achieved, would further improve the region’s investment climate. No change in Asia. We retain long CNHIDR and SGDIDR, where strong external balances, tight FX management, and ample intervention capacity provide insulation during periods of high uncertainty. In the February meeting, we think the BoK tried to manage expectations to curb aggressive market pricing of rate hikes (see Bank of Korea: Managing expectations, dated 26 February). For instance, the BoK introduced its new forward guidance in which more board members saw a rate cut rather than a hike in the next six months. Despite raising its 2026 GDP growth forecast, the BoK lowered its forecast for 2027. Given South Korea’s still-negative output gap amid a K- shaped economic recovery, we think the BoK will patiently assess the Middle East conflict’s impact to its policy variables, including growth, inflation and financial stability, rather than rush to adjust policy rates. However, a prolonged period of higher global oil prices and USDKRW could make balancing growth, inflation and financial stability tougher for the BoK. In this scenario, we think the BoK could prioritise inflation and financial stability. Still, our base case remains that the BoK will keep policy rates unchanged at 2.50% in 2026 and 2027. Agreement between State Street’s Foreign Exchange Holding Indicator (FXHI) and Foreign Exchange Hedge Ratio Indicator (FXHRI) enhances a positioning-driven view for developed market currencies. Because the impact of flows on future returns also depends on the positions of institutions in that currency, the FXHRI is, with the FXHI, designed to quantify and measure empirically this aspect of investor behaviour. The indicator is updated on a daily basis with a two -day publication lag. We publish foreign currency hedge ratios against multi-asset portfolios and are able to disaggregate this multi -asset hedge ratio into hedges against equity assets and fixed income assets. FX Behavioural Factor Flows and Factor Holdings measure real-money demand for and positioning in FX factors. At a high level, the indicators reveal whether real -money investors are leaning into or leaning out of a given FX factor (e.g. carry, value, momentum). records.text: nergy consumption), an indirect effect (i.e. through an increase in input prices for everything else, which gets to final consumer prices with a lag), and second-round effects (that work through expectations and wage formation). Indirect and second-round effects were negligible in the 2010s, with margins being the main variable of shock absorption. This was not the case throughout 2022 and 2023. In this particular case we would expect the ECB to look through only small and not very persistent oil price shocks. Indeed, with inflation expected to be below target for the next two years a small and not too persistent oil price shock would not substantially change this outlook, since the slightly higher inflation in the near term would be compensated by the deteriorated growth outlook in the medium term. And, if the growth impact was felt quickly, we could even see cuts already from the ECB in 2H26, earlier than expect, potentially even to a lower terminal rate. A permanent or large shock could be different though. The ECB could easily worry about sizeable indirect effects and second round effects. The shock could easily lead to later cuts than we expect (1H27). And under some scenarios we could even see a small number of hikes to make sure expectations remail well behaved. Both cases would likely be followed by deeper cuts than we expect right now.

The question arises as to what extent this will dampen the expected recovery of the manufacturing sector in Germany . We believe that German industry is nowadays fairly insulated from oil price shocks, for a number of reasons. Gases and electricity dominate here. LLC Global Economics Comment: Global Economic Impacts of the War in Iran 5 March 2026 | 12:39AM EST In this Global Economics Comment we evaluate the impact of the war in Iran on n global growth, inflation, and policy rates. The main economic impact for most countries is that the recent rise in oil prices n to around $80/bbl will boost inflation and slow growth. Applying our standard rules of thumb with our commodities team’s updated forecast implies a 0.2pp boost to global inflation (with core inflation impacts <0.1pp) and 0.1pp drag on global growth. Effects could be larger if the Strait of Hormuz closes for an extended period. We also see upside inflation risks from potential disruptions to LNG supply and heightened inflation expectation sensitivity. The macro data until 27 February, including latest PMIs (here) or February HICP inflation (here), were in line this view. But the events of the weekend have changed the calculus. The range of possible outcomes for inflation in the next months has considerably widened in the context of the US-Iran conflict. Given the recent increase in energy prices, euro area inflation will likely be back above the ECB's target for the remainder of this year. For 2027, inflation could fall again below target, but this is predicated on rapid energy market normalisation. In this environment, we think the ECB will be unwilling to cut rates and we expect it to stay on hold in 2026. In our view, a normalisation in energy markets will also put rate cuts back on the table, but only in 2027. Morgan Global Economics Contrib. to global CPI Brent oil Oil: Base: $60-55 fundamental Alt (dash): $80 Not too worried about worry A pillar of our 2026 outlook was the observed “fading of cau- tion” regarding US policy. Early-year data suggested that businesses were finally moving past the paralysis in hiring and non-tech capex and beginning to deploy their resilient profits and capital. This nascent recovery is now at risk. A military war, layered on top of the ongoing US “war on trade,” could reignite concerns over global stability. Experience suggests that business sentiment is not sensitive to energy supply shocks in the range described here (Figure 2). The interpretation of January matters. One is the low sample response rate. The BLS attributed some of this to the winter storm the week following the survey reference week when interviews are conducted. That may have meant a disproportionate number of initial interviews were done, called "month-in-sample" 1, or MIS-1. There are reasons that could be a slight (very slight) downward bias. The larger risk is that models of the unemployment rate, whether in levels or changes, depend heavily on the lagged unemployment rate. If the sampling creates noise that affected the January unemployment rate, that adds to the noise in the projection. Second, we expect some of the January drop in the unemployment rate is due to residual seasonality. We made that point last month in our preview. In each of the preceding three years, some, if not all, of that downward pressure from January unwinds in February (see chart of changes in the unemployment rate by month). Looking at the seasonal factors, seasonal flows and historical patterns we think expecting that again is justified. However, it could be wrong. In most EM economies, inflation is more sensitive to supply-driven energy price shocks than in DM because energy and food comprise a larger share of the CPI basket (see page 6). Consequently, the near-term inflationary impact of a sudden energy-price spike tends to outweigh the negative growth effect, especially when the shock is accompanied by a strong US dollar. This dynamic pushes EM central banks toward a more cautious stance in the short run, and, if energy-price pressures continue to intensify, the EM–DM rate differential would be likely to widen further. Our views imply it would be preferable to trim exposure to EM ‘receivers’ (i.e. reduce EM duration) than try to hedge it by adding ‘payers’ in G4 curves. We estimate that a 10% rise in global oil prices may lead to a 0.1–0.2pp reduction in GDP growth, while increasing CPI inflation by 0.2–0.3pp. As such, the Middle East tensions pose downside risks to our current 2026 growth forecast of 2.3%, and upside risks to our 2026 headline CPI forecasts of 2.2% (South Korea and Taiwan: AI-led growth momentum, dated 9 February). Other factors could also affect South Korea’s inflation – for instance, a 10% rise in USDKRW may lead to a 0.3pp increase in CPI inflation with the weakness likely to magnify should currency depreciation last longer. Moreover, a rise in shipping costs could add to inflation concerns via pass-through to core-goods inflation. Separately, we note that this would come amid a sharp rise in producer-price inflation for memory chips, which was one of the drivers for the Bank of Korea’s upward revision to its CPI forecasts during the February meeting. We think the government may utilise policy measures to mitigate the impact on inflation. For instance, the government has provided domestic refiners access to its oil reserves (which are enough for roughly seven months) to limit any disruption to industrial production. The government could also consider increasing fuel tax cuts – currently 7% for gasoline and 10% for diesel – which are set to expire by end-April. records.text: Asia Viewpoint | 03 March 2026 3 In addition to the potential spike in price, Asia could also bear the brunt from disruption in oil supply. Compared to Europe and US, Asia imports relatively more from the Middle East. Notably, Japan and Philippines import more than 90% of oil from Middle East, with many economies importing an average of 70% of oil from this region (Exhibit 3). It implies that in the case of any oil shipment suspension from the Hormuz Strait that lasts for weeks or months, these economies will likely have to divert trade and/or shift towards deploying their oil reserves. With 44% of oil imports coming from the Middle East, China will probably have to fall back on alternative oil sources in the short term, and rely more on its coal reserves as well as developing sustainable energy in the medium term. Even small disruptions at Hormuz—through which 21mn b/d of oil and 20% of global energy LNG volumes transit— could have outsized price effects and contribute to an initial spike in prices, with a multi week slowdown adding $5– $10/bbl. A prolonged shutdown could add as much as $40–$80/bbl to the Brent market. Meanwhile, targeted attacks on major regional facilities, or a collapse in Iran’s output, could move prices by $10–$50/bbl. Historical precedents from Libya, Syria, and Iraq suggest that military interventions often lead to long lasting supply disruptions. Limited global but heterogenous stagflation shock Historically, oil price spikes have been stagflationary shocks. However, oil dependency and oil sensitivity have changed significantly relative to the past, in particular in the US. In addition, initial conditions are important, and the US is still outperforming other DM and is now a net energy exporter. And oil importers like Japan, China and Europe are operating with negative output gap, which somewhat limits the inflationary shock. The other important dimension is how protracted the shock will be. If perceived as short-lived, the effects would be more limited. Our base case is a temporary spike of $10-$15 dollars in oil prices. This would have limited impact on inflation and activity in the US, though there is a relatively strong correlation between oil prices and inflation expectations. At the same time, across the Atlantic, US Oil & Gas (XOP) versus US Airlines (JETS) is overbought by 3.5 z-scores (16.8% from fair value). We think that in the event of a de-escalation, there could be an opportunity to fade these mispricings, which we will keep tracking. Higher oil prices directly increase inflation, often worsened by currency depreciation, which further raises local fuel costs. For countries that subsidize energy, these shocks add fiscal strain through higher spending. While importers are more exposed, even exporters may struggle with the second -round effects on inflation expectations and domestic demand. However, emerging markets have some key buffers: fuel prices have declined ov er the past year, and subsidies have gradually been cut, limiting fiscal impact from oil shocks. records.text: Main shock through oil and trade The impact on Asia should be mostly felt through the disruptions of oil and trade channels with heterogenous impact across different countries, in addition to risks from financial condition tightening and remittance declines. If oil prices remain elevated for a sustained period of time, Asia as a whole (as an oil importer) will likely witness downward pressure on growth and balance of payments. In particular, countries with more than 50% import oil supplying coming from the Middle East, such as Thailand, Philippines, India, Korea, Japan, and China, should be the first ones to feel the brunt. While we expect the inflation impact to be partially cushioned in countries with fuel-price smoothing mechanism, it will unlikely be fully offset. If the oil shock is substantial in magnitude and long-lasting in duration, the risks of CPI inflation being pushed up to levels that exceed central bank targets would rise, with additional risk of fiscal squeeze through fuel subsidies. Secondly, the choking point of Hormuz Strait shipment will also threaten to disrupt trade, push up shipping costs and insurance premium, as well as to test the supply chain of LNG and chemicals. The temporary closure of the strait not only leaves a gap of tens of millions barrels of oil supply for Asia, but also to extend general trade shipment with Middle East and Europe by more than 10 – 12 days at much higher shipping costs. As we highlighted last week (see more details in Cold Front Hits GSE Portfolio Growth), the unexpectedly slow portfolio growth in January following the announcement of the $200bn purchase program by President Trump on January 8 can be explained by two primary factors. First, the deceleration appears to be a partial return to seasonal patterns, as our analysis of the last five years confirms that portfolio growth in January is typically weaker than in December, likely due to the roll activities. Second, a delay in trade settlements likely played a key role. With the new purchase program announced on January 8, 2026, it is probable that the bulk of the subsequent purchasing activity was scheduled for a February settlement, meaning the full market impact is not yet visible in the January data. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 504/03/2026 Back to the future: The textbook central-bank response to a supply-driven rise in energy prices is to do nothing. After all, a temporary and relative price shift driven by external forces is not something that central bank policy can or should do much about. Given that for many economies this represents an adverse terms-of-trade shock, the disinflationary impulse from weaker economic activity could lean against higher energy prices. Beyond the macroeconomics of energy prices, elevated uncertainty also calls for central banks to tread cautiously. Series of shocks: This textbook line of reasoning relies, crucially, on inflation expectations being well anchored. We think this assumption is questionable, in light of the pandemic, energy shocks and more recently (and primarily in the US) tariffs. The high-inflation episode of the 1970s is an example of a series of inherently transitory supply shocks ultimately cumulating to destabilise inflation expectations. Starting points matter: What’s more, we think several other factors are important: underlying macroeconomic conditions, including the starting point for inflation (with below-target economies having more ‘space’ to absorb an increase); the reaction function of the central bank (i.e. dual mandate vs a singular focus on inflation); and the current policy setting. records.text: . A persistent spike in oil prices exposes the global economy to a risk of stagflationary shock. A related issue is the US vs China race to influence chokepoints: the US has incentives to increase control of strategic energy supply and advanced chip technology, to counteract China’s dominance in rare earth minerals. Developments from now until the Trump-Xi meeting in April will be key to watch beyond the very fluid dynamics of the US-Iran conflict. Limited global inflation shock, with EMEA most exposed EMEA is the most exposed region to energy price shocks, with an average share in the basket well higher than any other. Emerging Asia is also exposed but prices are less sensitive. Most DMs, including the US, are generally less sensitive to energy prices, somewhat limiting inflation risks. But the Euro Area’s and Japan’s exposure to energy is more elevated. Besides oil, shipping prices could spike again in the short term. As with the conflict in the Red Sea, this may most significantly impact Asia-Europe routes. For growth, focus on ToT, beware wealth effects in the US The impact on growth depends on the terms of trade, but we think it should be a moderate negative for the global economy in central scenarios. For the US, which has become a net energy exporter, we see the shock to growth from oil prices as muted, but we should watch shipping prices and most importantly any potential negative wealth effects from an eventual stock market correction. We think the shock is unlikely

Solar slowdown but new targets renew optimism: The rapid expansion of the Chinese solar industry has provided support to aluminium, now accounting for around 10% of China's aluminium demand, but the introduction of the renewable power trading mechanism last year, and the upcoming abolition of the photovoltaic (PV) export tax rebate in April dampens the outlook. Our China Utilities team sees a near-term peak in annual installations in 2025 at 315 GW, with 2026 installations expected to decline 27% to 230 GW. This implies a 26% YoY reduction in aluminium demand to ~3.5 Mt, this year. Going forward, China is targeting 3.6 TW of combined wind and solar capacity by 2030, versus 1.7 TW today. That implies a combined solar and wind installation rate of 190 GW/ year compared to 290/350/300 GW for 2023/24/25 YTD, suggesting a slowdown ahead. However, renewed growth could come from China's target to install 15 GW of concentrated solar power (CSP) by 2030, up from the ~1.7 GW currently installed, as CSP's aluminium intensity is >2x that of PV cells, which have previously dominated China's solar industry. records.text: 2 Japan Watch | 02 March 2026 Japan’s vulnerability to the escalation in the Middle East Geopolitical conditions in the Middle East deteriorated sharply after the U.S. and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on 28 February. While our Global Economics team does not expect a protracted conflict in its base case and assumes that the resulting rise in crude oil prices will be limited to $10–15/bbl, it assesses tail risks as much bigger than in June 2025 (see Global Economic Viewpoint: Iran: A chokepoints story 1 March). Japan is vulnerable to the escalation in the Middle East, as it relies on imports for nearly 100% of its crude oil, with more than 90% sourced from the region (Exhibit 1-Exhibit 2). Growth: A modest downside risk Japan’s exports to Iran account for only around 0.01% of total exports, and even including the Middle East as a whole, the share is only 4.2% of total exports (0.7% of nominal GDP, CY2025). Thus, the negative impact on Japan’s economy through a decline in exports is expected to be limited. On the other hand, as noted above, Japan relies on the Middle East for the most of its crude oil imports. Supply-chain disruptions related to crude oil imports and higher crude oil prices represent downside risks to the Japanese economy. records.text: BSL software: HY Energy crisis a guide for local impairment without a broad default cycle. Since late January, the selloff in software loans has extended meaningfully, with prices down another two points since we first covered the move about a month ago. The key question for investors is when this repricing translates into credit impairment—via negative ratings drift and, ultimately, defaults. Our baseline outlook remains benign, and we do not think the market is on the cusp of a broad-based default cycle. That said, we do think credit deterioration is likely to be more pronounced locally within software, and the 2015–16 HY Energy episode offers a useful analogue for how a sector-specific shock can unfold against an otherwise sound macro backdrop. At the time, Energy represented roughly 15–16% of the USD HY index—similar in magnitude to software’s footprint in BSL today—and the default cycle was highly concentrated: the trailing 12-month, issuer-weighted default rate for Energy issuers peaked near 33% in January 2017 while the broad HY default rate rose to about 8% (the 88th percentile since 2000). By contrast, the default rate excluding Energy issuers was only 3.7% (Exhibit 4). Meanwhile, investors looking for “fundamental confirmation” should keep in mind that market pricing tends to lead the data. Simulations of the Fed staff’s model of the US economy (FRBUS) from 2018 indicate d that a $20 oil price shock – similar to that observed recently – would have a small impact on growth (see here). The peak effect is only about a one-tenth drag on the level of output one year ahead. The impact on the unemployment rate is about half. A $60 oil price shock would have larger effects – given the linear nature of the model the impact is three times the $20 oil shock scenario. With oil prices around $120 per barrel, real GDP would be depressed by about 0.2 percentage points over a year and the unemployment rate would rise by a tenth. And we don’t think activity would be disrupted enough to meaningfully change the trajectory of the labor market. So we don’t expect the events in the Middle East to affect the trajectory of Fed policy. There are a few caveats to this relatively sanguine view. First, a large and sustained shock to energy prices might have non-linear effects on the economy. For example, a long-lasting 50% increase in crude oil prices might lower US growth by more than 50bp. Such a shock could also raise inflation expectations, which are typically sensitive to oil prices. This would make it harder for Warsh to push for cuts later this year. Second, meaningful tightening in financial conditions could exacerbate the shock. The economy is probably more sensitive than usual to markets. That’s because spending growth is being driven by higher-income households, who have benefited from a near- doubling in stocks over the last three years. A large and sustained equity downturn could weigh substantially on higher-income spending. Third, lower-income households are more exposed to oil price shocks, because energy makes up a larger share of their spending. These households are already struggling, so further erosion of their real spending power could cause another leg up in delinquencies (particularly credit cards and autos). Chinese authorities stated last year that they require average real GDP growth of only 4.17% in 2026–35 to accomplish the long-term goal of achieving ‘mid- developed countries’ status by 2035. That means annual 4.5% growth in 2026–30, and an 4% annual rate in 2031– 35, would be enough to fulfil this objective. That said, we do not rule out the possibility that the national target will be kept unchanged at 5.0% this year if the authorities are confident in the economy and believe they should aim higher. CPI target likely to remain 2%: All the 26 provinces that set quantitative CPI targets have kept them at 2.0% this year. This suggests that the national official CPI target will also remain 2.0%. It is worth highlighting that China’s inflation target is in fact the ceiling of the authorities’ inflation tolerance band, rather than the optimal rate that policymakers strive to achieve. In 2025, China’s headline CPI inflation was flat on a year-over-year basis, significantly below the 2.0% inflation target, but the PBoC did not react to the undershoot with materially more monetary easing. Instead, the PBoC cut interest rates by only 10bp last year, the smallest cuts since 2022. In the event, the Russian invasion generated a regional disrup- tion in natural gas markets, while not producing a global oil market “shock”. The immediate global macroeconomic outlook issue relates to the potential for a shock to the global supply of crude oil and natural gas. The regional concentration of global oil and gas supply flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and heightened uncertainties around the nature of the conflict point to elevat- ed tail risks. Channeled through our models, a sustained reduction of roughly one-fifth of this supply — in the range of 4mbd per day — would be sufficient to push Brent crude well above $100bbl. It will take time to understand the consequences of this con- flict, but tail risk concerns around supply disruptions will likely persist for some time. As such, we consider here an alternative scenario that sees oil prices remaining elevated through 1H26 before falling back to fundamental value around $60 through 2H26. As the current CDU-SPD regional government would no longer achieve a majority based on current polls, the most likely coalition options at the moment are a CDU-SPD-Green or a SPD-Left- Green government. On balance, unless oil prices remain persistently elevated, the domestic growth drag and underlying inflation implications would likely be modest and reinforce a cautious approach from the RBA rather than a material shift in the near-term policy outlook. Korea: risk for inflation and subsidies Similar to that of Japan, Korea relies heavily on crude oil imports from the Middle East (about 70% of the oil imports), of which over 95% volume transited the strait. About 20% of LNG imports also come from the region. A prolonged closure could disrupt domestic energy supply and shipping schedules, and to notably lifting domestic logistics, raw materials, electricity, gasoline, and diesel prices in Korea. That said, other than the higher energy prices, the near-term direct impact could be containable. The current oil reserves from both government and private sectors still at around 7-months of stockpiles, preventing any major supply issues in the short-term. In addition, other than energy sector, we also see relatively contained export exposure to the region. In terms of inflationary pressures, we expect Korea to face stronger cost push inflation in the coming months, driven not only by elevated oil prices but also by rising memory chip prices that are feeding into higher consumer electronics costs. Given these pressures, we see a strong likelihood that the government will continue deploying targeted energy subsidies to help contain near term inflationary momentum

(↑) Surging oil prices and shipping disruptions with renewed conflicts in the Midde East present a further upside risk for US inflation, adding to recent pressures on various goods prices. Of course, the magnitude and timing of inflationary impacts is very dependent on how long disruptions last. The largest impact will be on headline inflation via higher gas prices. A rough rule of thumb is that a ~10% move in oil prices would correspond to a ~5% move in retail gas prices, translating to around a 20bp boost to headline CPI. Increases in other energy prices such as natural gas could have additional moderate impacts. Pass through of higher energy prices to core inflation should be more limited, but upside risks would become more pronounced the longer disruptions last. Airfares are typically the most energy-exposed component of core inflation as higher jet fuel prices are passed on to higher ticket prices, especially over a longer period when costs may not be hedged by airlines. Higher energy costs, shipping disruptions, and possibly higher insurance costs could all create upward pressure on various goods prices as well. The timing and magnitude of higher core goods prices is very hard to estimate. Which way it goes will depend on the magnitude of the price action, its duration, and the extent to which oil/gas supplies remain disrupted. Emerging markets have benefited from a prolonged period of subdued inflation, with accommodative monetary policy supporting growth across the region. However, this benign backdrop is increasingly at risk of reversing. Rising oil prices —driven by heightened geopolitical tensions —alongside renewed USD strength could weaken local currencies and lift import-led inflation pressures. Over the past 12 months, the EM Fuel PriceStats monthly series remained in contraction, delivering one of its lowest annual reading s since 2023. This has been an important tailwind for EM economies, particularly in Asia and EMEA, where many countries are net oil importers. That support is now fading. Early signals point to a sharp acceleration in fuel prices, with aggregate EM fuel in flation rising to 1.6%m/m in February 2026. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

Conversely, during periods of deepening risk‑off sentiment, low‑yielding currencies tend to be bought. As a result, the yen is likely to weaken against the U.S. dollar and Swiss franc, while strengthening against currencies of energy‑importing countries and high‑beta currencies. However, if elevated oil prices persist, the yen is likely to weaken against the dollar as well as against the currencies of non‑Middle Eastern energy‑exporting countries. If USDJPY rises primarily due to broad‑based dollar strength, unilateral yen‑buying intervention by Japan is likely to be less effective. Authorities are therefore likely to adopt a wait‑and‑see stance for the time being. 02 March 2026 Economics Japan Takayasu Kudo Japan Economist BofAS Japan +81 3 6225 8592 takayasu.kudo@bofa.com Shusuke Yamada, CFA FX/Rates Strategist BofAS Japan +81 3 6225 8515 shusuke.yamada@bofa.com BoJ: Bank of Japan Accessible version Timestamp: 02 March 2026 07:12AM EST Unauthorized redistribution of this report is prohibited. If the AfD entered a regional government for the first time ever, this would likely create negative headlines (at home and abroad) and potentially have a negative impact on Germany as an investment location (at least for these two small regions). Reform momentum at the national level (e.g., with respect to pension reform) might stall for a couple of weeks until this new political reality is digested. Beyond the immediate reaction, lasting repercussions for overall economic sentiment and national policy making would likely be limited, in our view. Both, the CDU and the SPD, would probably try to frame this as regional specifics and prevent difficult regional government formation from spilling over to the national level. Conclusion The preceding analysis argue s that the recent rise in oil prices would likely have only a modest impact on the economic outlook – growth would be mildly lower and unemployment slightly higher. The most notable impact is on headline inflation but that may be treated as “transitory”. Risk scenarios in which oil moves significantly higher cannot be ruled out and would be commensurately higher. In response to this shock, Fed models suggest the Fed should undertake a somewhat more dovish posture and that 10 -year Treasury yields should broadly follow the contours of the Fed’s response. However, a key variable dictating the direction of the Fed’s re sponse will be whether inflation expectations begin to rise. The current backdrop of persistently above-target inflation over the past five years adds to the risk of inflation expectations potentially becoming unanchored if energy prices remain persistentl y elevated. For this reason, we see higher energy prices driven by tensions in the Mideast as reinforcing the Fed’s “wait - and-see” approach for the time being. Provided

As a result, instead of applying 2.5 million jobs of upward pressure, it applied only 2.383 million jobs of upward pressure. Earnings impact of oil price spike should be manageable but depends on duration To gauge the potential fundamental impact of the current conflict on Asian equities, we assess a $20/bbl oil supply shock on regional earnings. Refreshing our analysis from the outbreak of the Russia/Ukraine war, we group the region and individual market sectors into three buckets, which are (1) positively impacted by higher oil prices (e.g. oil & gas E&P), (2) negatively impacted by higher oil (e.g. chemicals, refinery, transportation, staples, autos, utilities), and (3) where the impact is broadly neutral (e.g. tech, financials, conglos, retails, healthcare, telcos). We then run a VAR (vector autoregression) analysis to capture both the oil supply shock and the indirect impact on earnings through potential economic growth effects. For the region as a whole, we estimate a $20/bbl rise in oil prices could reduce 2026 MXAPJ index earnings by a bit less than 2%. Given their respective macro sensitivities and sector weights, Philippines, Malaysia, and India could be impacted most while Thailand, Australia, and Indonesia could be more resilient. North Asian markets lie in the middle of the distribution. Importantly, this analysis assumes oil prices remain elevated. Our commodity analysts’ base case is that the current price spike will be short lived. The biggest effect is via oil prices. And even this channel has become less salient because the US is now a net exporter of oil and gas. Any headwind to consumers from higher energy prices should be partially offset by a windfall for energy producers. Energy goods and services account for less than 4% of US consumer spending. About half of that is gasoline. Accounting for the pass-through from crude oil to energy and other inflation components, the Federal Reserve Board estimates that a 10% increase in crude oil prices would raise PCE inflation by nearly 10bp in the near term. This effect would fade over the course of a year, as higher oil prices would weigh on demand for other goods and services. We estimate that the headwind to consumer spending would be similar to the upside to inflation. What about other components of GDP? The BEA estimates that petroleum and coal products make up about 1% of total value added across industries. Putting everything together, we estimate that a 10% increase in energy prices would weigh on US GDP by no more than 10bp. Initiating long USD 5y5y inflation: Our MarFA Macro model has highlighted in recent weeks an increased deviation between USD 5y5y inflation and its systemic fair value. This weekend’s events saw the deviation cross the −2 z-score threshold (around −8bp), suggesting USD 5y5y inflation is now significantly too low. USD 5y5y inflation and oil prices have historically been correlated (Figure 4). This correlation seems to have fallen since the middle of last year, however, perhaps driven by market expectations for a normalisation in US economic growth and long-term lower oil prices. The focus on Middle East events and prospect of higher- for-longer oil prices opens scope for USD 5y5y inflation to recouple with its fair value, we argue. As a result, we initiate a long 5y5y inflation trade idea, targeting 2.48%. A weakening in US economic data, as highlighted by our FCI-led projections, could act as a risk to this trade. We note that 10y breakeven is not as cheap as 5y5y, while 5y inflation appears slightly rich. During the oil price spike linked to the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine 5y5y inflation initially declined before moving higher with 5y breakeven inflation. The performance of the HY factors was largely consistent with what we would expect when spreads are moving wider. With output above the lower threshold, this leaves no room for meaningful future growth, ending China's rapid expansion that saw production increase from 12.6 Mt in 2007 to now. This has been reflected in China's 2025 trade balance with annual imports (primary, alloys, scrap and semis) up 400 kt YoY, while exports were down 510 kt, implying a ~910 kt reduction in net exports. China pivoting to upgrades and capacity exports: We expect the capacity cap to hold this year with any production growth likely to be incremental as producers prioritise internal replacement and a shift toward higher amperage technology. records.text: We can take these estimated shifts in the net energy balance (as a % of GDP) and calculate the likely FX adjustment in real trade-weighted terms that would help re-balance the current account through our GSFEER model. This is a simple exercise that assumes the other inputs of our model remain constant and does not account for other factors that may impact FX markets (such as risk premium or FX interventions, for example). Still, it can be a helpful benchmark of how current account pressures can impact these currencies (we carried out a similar exercise for EUR in 2022). The largest impact under our scenario is on NOK where a ~4ppt current account increase is associated with nearly 10% real trade-weighted appreciation. Even without this added boost, the Krona is already close to 12% undervalued in our FEER model given its large current account surplus. But crucially for NOK, Norway’s unique fiscal mechanism requires that the Norges Bank intervene in FX markets to account for excess energy sector revenues, which effectively insulates the currency from much of the shift in European energy prices and Norway’s current account. We also saw this dynamic at play in 2022 where a large current account increase did not translate into sustained NOK appreciation. Elsewhere, if current oil and gas prices are sustained, HUF and PLN would have to depreciate the most (around 1.8%) to offset the deterioration in their respective current accounts followed by EUR, SEK and GBP . Over the medium to long term, these developments would further reinforce the Takaichi administration’s push to strengthen Japan’s energy and national security policies. Australia: Oil importer, LNG exporter Australia is a net importer of oil and refined fuels, but large exporter of LNG and bulk commodities. An oil price and trade flow shock would weigh on external demand and export volumes, but a lower AUD (common in a risk-off environment) and spillovers to other commodity prices (eg LNG) may cushion the hit to exporter incomes and domestic growth. Higher petrol prices would squeeze disposable incomes and weigh on household discretionary consumption, while firm margins and investment may also be adversely affected. Summary of Updated Forecasts We summarise all the above changes to our 2026 forecasts (reflected in our new baseline scenario) in Exhibit 6. Duration Matters As mentioned above, in our new base case scenario, the disruption to oil flows is short-lived while the price impact relative to our previous forecasts is significant, meaning that price effects outweigh volume effects in determining economic outcomes. As a result, the impact on fiscal and external balances is likely to be relatively benign (if not positive) across the board. However, the more prolonged the disruption to oil flows, the more important volume effects become relative to price effects. The price adjustment required to compensate for the output loss increases exponentially, particularly for those countries with less potential to divert oil exports. As such, the duration of disruption also results in a more uneven impact across GCC countries. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. Regional risk/reward: manage downside while remaining strategically positive The current environment reinforces one of our key themes for 2026, which is managing risk while staying engaged in regional markets. Over the past four decades, the regional index has averaged a 10% or greater correction every 8-9 months. Currently, the MXAPJ index has risen over 60% since last April (nearly 11 months) without more than a 7% pullback. Our regional Asia drawdown risk model (RADaR) flags a high probability of a moderate pullback and our Markov regime switching model shows a degree of complacency because valuation volatility is low despite more elevated geopolitical risk. Heightened geopolitical uncertainty together with risk of some negative oil-related earnings impact if the Mideast conflict persists underscores the merit of derivative hedging strategies that enhance positive return asymmetry. These include downside put structures and upside cash replacement strategies. February began unusually cold, but turned milder in the establishment survey reference week. When accounting for this, the models still imply a weather boost for February. While it was warmer than typical in Memphis, 62 degrees on February 12, on the East Coast it was unseasonably cold still, 36 and 38 degrees in New York and Washington, D.C. The lasting impact via erosion of confidence, particularly given the large expatriate populations in these countries, remains to be seen. Long-term diversification strategies: A prolonged conflict could deal a further 3. blow to global perceptions of the region’s structural geopolitical stability. This may have a more long-term detrimental effect on regional diversification strategies, which by and large depend on expanding tourism and attracting foreign direct investment into strategic sectors, such as tech (AI), finance and manufacturing. The extent to which this is true in the long term will depend on the geopolitical environment that emerges post-conflict, and it is too early to say with confidence what this will be. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 02 March 2026 5 The direct impact of military conflicts is obviously negative for the geographies where the conflict takes place. For the broader Middle East, the conflict could be harmful to the extent the region was emerging as an alternative hub for new business, but risk premium could significantly rise amid retaliatory attacks from Iran on US allies in the region. Elsewhere, it depends on a combination of terms of trade, fiscal, and monetary policy. In the US, fiscal policy typically becomes expansionary, and the composition of growth shifts away from private consumption and investment. But for a conflict that is not very protracted, the negative shock to US growth and its composition would be modest. However, in a context of a K-shaped economy with elevated stock market valuations, we should closely watch for any wealth effects emanating from a market correction. This argument is likely most relevant for the US, but applies more broadly, as stock indexes across the world are generally near record levels. Diverse implications for central banks While this is a supply shock, we believe some central banks may be more cautious than others to prevent inflation from getting entrenched, especially those in EM that are witnessing some renewed inflationary pressures. The government may rely on state-owned utilities such as BOTAS and TEDAS or on tax adjustments to absorb wholesale energy price spikes and limit the pass-through to household electricity and gas bills, helping to contain overall inflation pressures. The central bank is estimating that a 10% jump in energy prices can push headline CPI around a full percentage point higher (with almost half of this jump materialising within the first quarter of the shock). Adding in second round effects of higher energy into food and via a weaker currency, the impact could be north of 2pp to headline CPI over the coming months assuming the current level of oil and gas prices. records.text: Energy Price Shock Leaves Risks to Dollar Around NFP More Symmetric While focus has been on the Middle East, and any renewed rally in energy prices should be the dominant factor for markets, the growth and rate implications from any surprise in tomorrow’s US labor market report should still be a key driver of relative FX performance. A beat looks likely to ease US growth concerns, even if downside risk remains from a prolonged global energy price shock. Meanwhile, a miss should raise US growth concerns, and likely more so than previous reports given the interaction with lingering risks around energy prices and AI disruption. The extent to which the NFP report affects global growth expectations will determine whether the Dollar strengthens or weakens against high-beta FX (e.g., AUD, NZD, Scandis, MXN, ZAR). We introduced an FX playbook for NFP last year, based on the price action of a set of currencies in the 30 minutes post release over the prior 12 reports. On average, the Dollar had largely traded as a procyclical currency around the releases, underperforming both G10 and EM FX on misses and outperforming (to a smaller and more narrow extent) on beats. The playbook has continued to hold, as we find a similar pattern when shifting to a more recent sample covering the reports for January 2025 through January 2026 (Exhibit 1). We also find a generally similar pattern in the price action following just the last two reports, for December 2025 and January 2026 (Exhibit 2). Howeve

records.text: l prices had become more sensitive to nationwide cost shocks such as swings in gasoline prices and exchange rates. The second paper builds on this finding. Specifically , and especially relevant for today, it uses the 2022 energy price spike after the outbreak of war in Ukraine as a case study . Alberto and his co-authors show that the frequency of price adjustments more than doubled after the shock, leading to a swift pass-through of higher costs into consumer prices. They use the case study to challenge the s tandard time - dependent pricing models , which usually assume firms change prices at a fixed intervals and are unable to capture sudden inflation surge s. Instead, the authors demonstrate that a state -dependent pricing framework, where firms reprice whenever large cost changes erode profit margins, fits the data and explains the more rapid pass-through. Figure 1: Duration of regular price changes (months) Source: Amazon Effects (Oct-2018) The key implication is that large shocks can produce faster and more pronounced inflation than in normal times, underscoring the limitations of traditional sticky -price models. For inflation forecasting and monetary policy, the results highlight the importance of incorporating state -dependent price-setting behavior to avoid underestimating the inflationary impact and to better anticipate the speed of price hikes after major supply shocks. records.text: US Economic Perspectives5 March 2026 ab 10 Temporary Protected Status (TPS): not much change Temporary Protected Status (TPS) allows individuals to live and work in the US legally if their home countries are deemed unsafe due to circumstances such as natural disasters, wars, or other "extraordinary and temporary" conditions, according to the Department of Homeland Security. According to the National Immigration Forum (link here), as of March 31, 2025, there were ~1.3 million individuals with TPS living in the US. Since September, the Trump administration terminated TPS for South Sudan and Myanmar, affecting ~3K individuals, and the 2021 designation for Venezuela, impacting 242K individuals. To date, the Trump administration has terminated or announced its intent to terminate TPS for over 1 million of the 1.3 million, with the most from Venezuela (~600K), Haiti (~330K) and Honduras (~50K). Several decisions are being challenged in court. The Supreme Court granted the administration's request to stay a lower-court ruling that had allowed ~350K Venezuelans (who received TPS under the 2023 re-designation) to maintain their status while litigation continues. The affected individuals would have lost TPS and reverted to their prior status effective November 7. records.text: M Idea 8 How Energy and AI Might Shape CPI Inflation Ahead Diego Anzoategui Supply-driven oil shocks: Short-run boost to headline, but limited impact on core Our previous work finds that a persistent 10% increase in oil prices driven by a negative supply shock raises headline CPI by about 35 bp for roughly three months, but boosts core CPI by only around 3 bp. The impact on core inflation is not only small but also highly narrow: historically, the pass-through occurs mainly through airfares. Absent a sharper rise in energy prices, the effects on core inflation tend to be short-lived and limited. This relatively modest impact on core inflation suggests that the Fed is likely to look through the near-term inflationary impulse from higher oil prices. If disruptions in oil markets intensify, uncertainty remains elevated, and oil prices rise above $100 for an extended period, the oil shock could ultimately weigh on the real economy and lead to visible deterioration in labor market conditions. In that scenario, the Fed could end up cutting rates more aggressively than we—and markets—currently expect. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. records.text: ublicly disclosed. While liquidity management is a complex process, we can try to simplify it for the purposes of this note. In its most high-level form, a bank has deposits, which can flow out during times of stress. To gauge how much liquidity is needed in times of stress, a bank has to make assumptions about how much of the deposits will flow out and at what speed. For example, when looking at institutional deposits, a bank has to make assumptions about how much of it is needed for operational reasons (i.e. payments that occur regularly and support business needs) versus how much is extra cash that is sitting in the account, with the idea being that excess cash can be deployed more quickly than operational cash. Therefore, a bank can make an assumption about how much of its wholesale deposits are operational versus non- operational and the speed at which they will flow out of the bank in times of stress. Similar assumptions about the pace and the amount of outflows can be made about retail deposits as well. To meet these outflows, banks hold high-quality assets (cash, USTs, Agency MBS), and banks have to make assumptions about how quickly they can monetize these securities as well. Cash is readily available, whereas securities must be monetized. This simple construct highlights the importance of day one liquidity. If a bank has a high concentration of deposits that it assumes will flow out on day one, or early on, it will need to hold some amount of cash, as it will have to assume that only a portion of the securities will likely be monetized on day one. This is likely the reason why banks have favored hold- ing reserves following the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) crisis (Figure 1), as that event illus- trated how quickly some deposits can leave. records.text: USD IG insurers: Recent widening looks overdone. A confluence of headlines around AI disruption and, more recently, private credit has pushed USD IG insurance spreads wider, with the move unfolding in two distinct legs—first in late January as the broader complex repriced on AI fears and then more sharply in life insurers as private credit concerns intensified (Exhibit 10). The market narrative centers on life insurers as a conduit for private credit risk and on the growing web of ownership and distribution ties between insurers and alternative asset managers. That said, our review of a representative sample of life insurers suggests balance sheet positioning is less aggressive than feared: the median allocation to alternatives is only 6% (Exhibit 11). Investors have instead focused on corporate credit—the largest asset class for these firms—where we estimate an average 22% allocation to “private securities” within the broader available-for-sale portfolio for insurers that disclose the split (again, Exhibit 11). Importantly, corporate bonds appear to represent a meaningfully smaller share of Level 3 fair-value assets—the least observable and most model-dependent bucket (Exhibit 12)—which suggests many holdings are more consistent with broadly distributed private placements (e.g., Rule 144A or Regulation S) rather than truly hard-to-price instruments. records.text: Liquidity holding up well despite the return of dispersion and volatility. Implied volatility on the CDX index has gone from the 7th percentile in early January to the 72nd percentile today vs. a history of the last 10 years. We have also recently highlighted the nascent return of dispersion to corporate credit markets. When volatility and dispersion resurge, concerns around market liquidity tend to surface. A review of our standard metrics of bid/ask spreads, Amihud, and turnover, continue to show a healthy market microstructure where risk intermediation is still functioning normally (Exhibits 59 and 60). One metric that is flashing yellow is net dealer positioning in the USD IG market which has dropped to unprecedentedly negative levels (Exhibit 13). While we used to track this measure closely as a barometer of market liquidity, in the current evolution of the market we would discount its usefulness for two reasons. First, the rise of portfolio trading has brought on a fundamental change to the way many clients trade corporate credit. Many of these trades are done via total return swaps (TRS) or ETFs, meaning that the way in which dealers source and inventory bonds has necessarily shifted. Second, the evolution in the broker/dealer model, from principal trading towards more agency trades has obviated the need to hold large inventories of corporate bonds on balance sheet. records.text: returns in 2025, driven in part by expectations of future AI-related productivity gains, appear to be supporting household balance sheets and confidence. This “productivity news” channel helps explain why consumer spending has remained resilient even as labor markets show signs of cooling. Stronger consumption, particularly in services, can sustain pricing power and delay the appearance of disinflation, even if underlying supply-side improvements are underway. Electricity prices represent a more concrete and measurable channel through which AI may raise near term inflation pressures. After the pandemic, electricity prices initially moved closely with natural gas prices, following them with a lag. When natural gas prices surged by roughly 125% during the Russia–Ukraine war, electricity prices rose as well. However, even after natural gas prices fell back, electricity inflation remained sticky at around 4–5% year over year. Given that natural gas is a primary input into electricity generation and historically leads electricity prices by about two quarters, this persistence suggests that demand side forces are keeping electricity inflation above its pre COVID trend.

A 10% rise in crude oil prices would push up Japan-style core CPI by a total of 0.1ppt via the energy CPI. In addition, higher logistics costs could exert inflationary pressure across a wider range of items. The subsequent impact will depend on the FX reaction, and evidence suggests that the pass-through from yen depreciation to CPI has recently strengthened. BoJ: Rising uncertainty now, inflation risks later Worsening geopolitical developments in the Middle East imply increased uncertainty around the global economy and financial markets for the BoJ in the near term. While it is unlikely that the BoJ would respond directly to higher energy prices through monetary policy, further yen depreciation could prompt the Bank to consider raising rates at a faster pace amid rising inflation concerns. Fiscal policy: Rising national security policy need A sharp surge in energy prices could raise the risk of the government reinstating fuel price-subsidy measures. Over the medium to long term, growing support within the LDP and among the broader public is likely to further bolster the administration’s efforts to advance its energy policy and national security agenda. At the beginning of the year we tend to see outflows from the USPS as holiday hiring is unwound, but these swings tend to be offset by seasonal adjustment. We are not expecting much SA change in the USPS in February. Between November and December, employment at the USPS rose 13K on a non-seasonally adjusted basis, then fell -10K in January. Given the flows in recent years, this could imply that the bulk of the holiday hiring unwind is behind us. We could see a small positive NSA contribution from the USPS in February, but view the risks to the SA change as two-sided this year. We expect state and local employment expanded in February with an improvement in local government employment offset by weakness, though less weakness, in state government employment. State and local government employment has contracted for three straight months with the 6-month moving average change at -6K in January, though that has been lumpy. The weight of this category is relatively low at ~ 0.3%. The impact of chip shortage on inflation depends on the extent of it. Our equity strategists note that "Memory remains a small share of vehicle cost but an outsized driver of operational risk. As DRAM content rises and legacy supply tightens, margin pressure is likely to build across the automotive supply chain, with structural redesign risk emerging if supply contraction persists." On growth, these estimates indicate that higher oil prices weigh on real incomes and spending, although oil exporters such as Canada and some Latin American economies should benefit. And on headline inflation, these estimates—which are highest for EM economies in Central and Eastern Europe and Asia—account for both the direct effects from higher energy prices as well as the indirect effects from higher production costs. We expect moderate consumption growth of 1.2% in 2026, amid a small fall in savings rates and slowing real income growth. This is before accounting for the recent rise in energy prices. Monetary easing and past and expected falls in interest rates can continue to reduce the motivation to pay down debt, hold savings and make it cheaper to borrow, causing a small decline in the savings rate. We expect savings rate to fall to 9.5% in 2026 from 10.1% in 2025. While the decline in inflation and rate cuts should act as tailwinds, real income growth is likely to slow amid softening wage growth and a looser labour market. At the same time, the recent rise in energy prices, if sustained, may slow the path of disinflation. The freeze in income tax thresholds is also likely to weigh on disposable incomes. Moreover, the number of fixed rate households potentially facing higher mortgage payments is expected to rise again and mortgage interest payments as a share of income is likely to rise marginally, after falling slightly in 2025, providing a marginal drag to consumption growth. Overall, we expect real disposable income growth to slow from 1.1% in 2025 to 0.6% to 2026 (Exhibit 6). The contribution of wages and salaries is likely to reduce in 2026 given weaker employment and pay growth, while net taxes are likely to a slightly bigger drag. records.text: FX Performance this Week Consistent with Typical Betas to Risk and Gas First, we benchmark the performance across European currencies so far this week against their typical sensitivities to shifts in energy prices and risk sentiment. Specifically, we narrow in on the impact of fluctuating European natural gas prices during shocks of this nature by taking key European crosses’ betas to moves in TTF and global equities on days (in a sample from January 2010 to February 2026) where Brent prices are at least $5/bbl higher. The resulting sample is concentrated around – but not exclusive to – the 2022 energy shock episode. This simple benchmarking exercise explains the week-to-date moves in European FX relatively well. This is particularly true for CEE currencies, where the clear underperformance as a bloc, led by HUF, tallies with both their high-beta properties and their large relative shares of net energy imports. In the G10 space, the energy and risk betas capture almost all of the week-to-date moves in EUR/USD and EUR/GBP – though on the latter, we think that an outsized reduction in BoE cut premium has also been a key driver of Sterling outperformance this week. The Scandi currencies, meanwhile, have shown less differentiated performance than this exercise would imply, with a full reversal in EUR/SEK to below Friday’s levels appearing particularly at odds with the much smaller retracements in TTF and global equities. If the oil shock turns out to be more than a transitory change, with oil prices plateauing at a much higher level for longer, most Asian economies will likely witness downward pressure on growth through terms of trade losses, along with higher inflation. Uneven oil import supply will be put to test We also note East Asian economies tend to have large shares of their oil imports coming from the Middle East, e.g. Japan at 95% and Philippines at 94%. With many economies importing an average of 70% of oil from this region, it implies that in the case of any oil shipment suspension from the Hormuz Strait that lasts for weeks or months, these economies will likely have to divert trade and/or shift towards deploying their oil reserves. With 44% of oil imports coming from the Middle East, China will probably have to fall back on alternative oil sources in the short term, and rely more on its coal reserves as well as developing sustainable energy in the medium term. Trade disruptions to go beyond shipping logistics The choke point of Hormuz Strait shipment will likely threaten to disrupt trade, push up shipping costs and insurance premium, as well as test the supply chain of LNG and petrochemicals. The temporary closure of the strait not only leaves a gap of tens of millions barrels of oil supply for Asia, but also to extend general trade shipment with Middle East by more than 10–12 days at much higher shipping costs. The learnt experience of the last couple of decades feeds into this, with the global economy demonstrating resilience to a variety of shocks. Indeed, as we wrote about last week, AI could matter far more for the macro economy longer-term. For now, the AI narrative in rates space is only masked, although it was never going to be priced in a straight line given the many unknowns. We concluded that the latest twists in the narrative outlook meant that the inflation pass though was modest and the outlook for inflation relatively benign. In March, using a similar combination of Alberto’s past papers, a recent case study and current State Street PriceStats data , the potential pass through from higher energy prices is much, much more so. Higher energy prices pose a bigger risk to the inflation outlook than tariffs, especially after the 2022/23 experience. Shocking papers Following a similar format to the tariff analysis we lean heavily on two Alberto papers, Amazon Effects (Oct-2018) and, Large shocks travel fast (Dec 2024). The first 2018 study shows that online competition , exemplified by Amazon’s algorithmic pricing and price transparency, has sharply increased the frequency of price changes for all US retailers . Price adjustments now occur much more often , implied price durations roughly halved over the prior decade (Figure 1). One of the supposedly most robust stylized facts of € rates of the post-GFC sample has been the tendency of Schatz spreads to richen when markets turn risk off. While long-run historical evidence doesn’t actually look that compelling (at least if we proxy risk-off via swings in short-expiry implied vol or EGB spread dispersion – Figure 8), it has certainly been the case that the reaction to the higher realized volatility in both swap rates and EGB spreads over the last week hasn’t been matched by richer Schatz spreads. records.text: Noel Dixon 4 March 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Digesting the n ew g eopolitical reality KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Making sense of it all. Investors began the week reassessing geopolitical risks following recent military action against Iran. While markets initially expecting a limited strike, the outlook now appears more prolonged and uncertain. President Trump has suggested the operation could last four to five weeks, while leaving open the possibility of an extension. Attention remains focused on potential Iranian retaliation, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz—a critical chokepoint through which 20–30% of global oil supply passes. The Iran Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has formally announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In response, WTI crude prices quickly moved back above $72/bbl. Over the weekend, OPEC+ announced a production increase of 206,000 barrels per day, but this is unlikely to offset a material disruption to flows through the strait. While OPEC+ holds roughly 3.7 million barrels per day of spare capacity, approximately 20 million barrels per day typically transit Hormuz. These developments come amid already-persistent inflation pressures in major economies—particularly the United States—which could complicate central banks’ ability to deliver the rate cuts currently priced by markets if the conflict persists.
